\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Correctness-Gated Reinforcement Learning for High-Frequency
DSP Accelerator RTL Generation, Validated on Silicon}

\author[hit]{Mohamed Amine Hallam}
\ead{hallamamine05@gmail.com}
\address[hit]{Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China}

\begin{abstract}
Large language models can now emit syntactically valid Verilog, but functional
correctness alone is not a useful engineering target: a register-transfer level
(RTL) description is only valuable if it is both correct and fast enough to
close timing on the target device. Existing work optimises these two objectives
separately, evaluates them with synthesis estimates rather than measurement, and
rarely distinguishes generalisation to unseen parameters from memorisation of
the training grid. This paper proposes a correctness-gated reinforcement
learning method in which the reward of a generated design is its predicted
maximum clock frequency \emph{if and only if} an input/output-equivalence oracle
certifies the design correct, and zero otherwise. The method is applied to five
families of single-input streaming digital signal processing (DSP) accelerators
spanning three circuit classes---multiply--accumulate datapaths, recursive
filters with real feedback, and multiplier-free comparator networks---and is
evaluated under a frozen held-out protocol that separates parameter
interpolation from extrapolation. On thirty held-out designs never seen during
supervised fine-tuning, policy optimisation, or surrogate training, the proposed
policy raises the mean timing-closed Vivado \fmax{} from $86.5$ to
$\best{211.3}$~MHz in the interpolation regime ($+144\%$) and from $78.5$ to
$\best{174.2}$~MHz in the extrapolation regime ($+122\%$), while exceeding a
perfect-selector best-of-eight baseline in both regimes. The same recipe
transfers without modification to a second base model, and both models converge
to the same measured frequency ceiling, indicating that the optimisation
recovers a property of the design rather than of the model. Five held-out design
pairs were placed on a Xilinx Zynq-7020 device and swept in hardware, where the
optimised designs sustain $2.25$--$3.40\times$ the measured clock of the
supervised baseline with zero spread across repeated runs. We further show that
saturation of the learned frequency surrogate is an observable early-warning
signal of reward hacking, exhibit one caught case in which a surrogate reported
$188.6$~MHz for a design that measures $36$--$40$~MHz on real hardware, and
report the two families where the method yields no frequency gain together with
the mechanism that explains it.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
Register-transfer level generation \sep Reinforcement learning \sep
Large language models \sep Field-programmable gate arrays \sep
Design space exploration \sep Reward hacking
\end{keyword}
